title: Meta open sources code to let you make Muse AI gadgets
content:
Meta now lets you make your own Muse gadgets that feature the company’s new AI agent with code that the company open sourced. The company suggests projects like loading Muse on a color E Ink display to show reminders, adding it to an HDMI stick so you can display Muse on a big screen, or putting Muse on a small touchscreen device to make what looks kind of like a DIY Muse Charm.
Meta open sources code to let you make Muse AI gadgets
Meta now lets you connect Muse to your own hardware to put on your displays or a Raspberry Pi.
“Muse gadgets are open source devices you build yourself,” Meta says. “Program an off-the-shelf ESP32 board or set up a Raspberry Pi with our SDKs, then connect Muse to your displays, buttons, sensors, actuators, and whatever else you’ve got lying on your workbench.” However, Meta cautions that you should “Proceed at your own risk!”
The company is also giving away a Muse Home Link gadget that it created. With the Muse Home Link, you use community-built skills to have the AI agent “turn on a light, control your TV, send a document to a printer, and more, depending on your setup,” Meta says. It manufactured 5,000 of the gadgets, according to Meta Superintelligence Labs’ Nat Friedman, and you can claim a waitlist spot for the Muse Home Link now ahead of shipping sometime this month.

report.summary: Meta open-sourced code and SDKs so developers can build DIY Muse AI gadgets on ESP32 or Raspberry Pi, and it's giving away 5,000 Muse Home Link devices.
report.background: AI assistants are moving beyond phone apps into ambient hardware, from smart speakers to wearable cameras. Meta has been expanding its AI footprint through Ray-Ban glasses, Quest headsets, and its Muse agent, while rivals like Amazon, Google, and Apple push their own home AI ecosystems. By open-sourcing SDKs for cheap boards like ESP32 and Raspberry Pi, Meta is trying to seed a developer community around Muse rather than control every device itself. The giveaway of 5,000 Muse Home Link units, announced by Meta Superintelligence Labs' Nat Friedman, tests demand for an agent that controls lights, TVs, printers, and other home gear. The cautious "proceed at your own risk" language shows this is an experimental, community-driven push.
key_points: Meta released open-source code and SDKs that let developers put the Muse AI agent on off-the-shelf hardware, including ESP32 boards and Raspberry Pi. Users can connect displays, buttons, sensors, and actuators to build custom AI gadgets, with Meta offering sample ideas like E Ink reminder screens and touchscreen DIY Muse Charms.

Meta suggests several projects: loading Muse on a color E Ink display for reminders, putting it on an HDMI stick for big-screen use, or building a small touchscreen device similar to a DIY Muse Charm. The approach turns cheap hobbyist hardware into potential AI agent interfaces.

Meta is also giving away 5,000 Muse Home Link gadgets. Through community-built skills, the device can turn on lights, control a TV, send documents to a printer, and more depending on a user's setup. A waitlist is open, with shipping expected this month.

The company warns users to "proceed at your own risk," signaling that these gadgets are experimental. That caveat highlights potential security, privacy, and reliability concerns when an AI agent connects to home hardware and personal devices.

Strategically, Meta is pushing Muse beyond its own apps and into physical spaces. Open-sourcing hardware code could attract makers, speed up experimentation, and help Meta compete with established smart-home assistants from Amazon, Google, and Apple.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Meta's move signals that the next assistant battle will happen in ambient hardware, not just chatbots. Open-source SDKs could commoditize AI gadget development, letting small teams and hobbyists build niche agents without big licensing deals. Developers gain low-cost ways to prototype voice, display, and sensor-driven AI experiences, but they must handle security, privacy, and maintenance themselves. Regular users may see a wave of quirky, personalized AI devices, yet also face fragmentation, limited support, and risks when an agent controls home equipment. If successful, Muse gadgets could pressure rivals to open their own platforms or tighten ecosystem lock-in.
report.tools: To follow along, watch Meta's Muse SDK and Home Link waitlist, plus ESP32 boards, Raspberry Pi, and ESPHome for DIY hardware. Home Assistant is useful for community skills and smart-home integration. Arduino IDE or PlatformIO can help with firmware, while color E Ink displays, HDMI sticks, and small touchscreens are common project parts.
